newsitem.title: FRANCE: France avoids endorsing U.S. raid on Iraq.
newsitem.headline: France avoids endorsing U.S. raid on Iraq.

text.p: France, one of the 1991 Gulf War allies, withheld support for a U.S. missile attack on Iraq on Tuesday, saying Baghdad had not breached U.N. resolutions by sending its troops into Kurdish areas of northern Iraq.

Foreign Minister Herve de Charette told reporters that Paris had been "informed of the American actions" but pointedly refrained from endorsing them. He reiterate France's support for Iraq's territorial integrity.
Syrian Foreign Minister Farouq al-Shara said after meeting de Charette that the two shared similar views. "Syria, like France, is very committed to the integrity of Iraqi territory," he said.

French officials said U.S. President Bill Clinton telephoned President Jacques Chirac on Monday night to inform him of the impending 27-missile attack on military targets in southern Iraq in retaliation for an offensive by President Saddam Hussein's troops against Kurdish areas of northern Iraq.
Chirac had made clear he understood Clinton's motives, in the midst of the U.S. presidential election campaign, but differed on the appropriateness and legality of military action.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry called the exchange "a useful, productive and candid discussion", suggesting there was some disagreement.
Implicitly challenging the legality of the U.S. raid, French Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said Paris did not believe the Iraqi offensive violated U.N. resolutions.

"We do not see that United Nations resolutions are called into question by the Iraqi intervention, especially since there was a written request by one of the main Kurdish movements. Iraq is acting entirely on its own soil," he told reporters.

The Iraqi government says the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) asked for military support against the rival Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), which it accused of having military backing from neighbouring Iran.
France fought alongside the United States in the Gulf War to drive Iraqi invasion forces out of Kuwait in 1991 and is one of the allies enforcing no-fly zones in southern and northern Iraq.
But as Iraq's biggest creditor and erstwhile arms supplier, it is keen to ease the U.N. economic embargo against Iraq.
The Foreign Ministry said France "took note" of Clinton's decision to extend the no-fly zone in southern Iraq to just south of Baghdad and was studying the implications.
By describing the extension of the zone as an "American decision", the statement suggested that while Paris had been consulted, it had not explicitly agreed.

De Charette said he sent a message to Iraqi Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz on Monday expressing concern for the safety of civilians and the hope that Baghdad would withdraw its forces as soon as possible.
The message said that only a dialogue between Baghdad and the Kurdish factions could lead to the restoration of stability through a political settlement.
Rummelhardt said France hoped a U.N.-brokered pact allowing Baghdad to sell limited quantities of oil in exchange for food would soon be implemented.
The United Nations said on Sunday it was delaying implementation to assure the safety of its staff and Washington said on Tuesday it wanted the deal changed.

French officials said the U.S. strike should be seen in the context of the U.S. presidential campaign. Clinton's Republican challenger Bob Dole had accused the Democratic president of weakness in his response to the Iraqi offensive.
The officials said that while Paris differed with Washington on the raid, Chirac would not publicly criticise Clinton, who is hot favourite to win re-election on November 5.
